meta.title: Colonial Pipeline Attack
meta.description: A model of the 2021 ransomware attack on the Colonial Pipeline Company (CPC)
meta.article: Malicious cyber actors acquired gained access to Colonial Pipeline's IT network and once in the system the MCAs deployed DarkSide ransomware and locked down the corporate IT system. On may 7th 2021 the Colonial Pipeline Company (CPC) learned they were victims of a ransomware cyber attack. In response CPC proactively took certain systems offline halting pipeline activity.

data.label: Pipeline Shutdown
user_properties:
On may 7th 2021 the Colonial Pipeline Company (CPC) 
learned they were victims of a ransomware cyber attack.

In response CPC "proactively took certain systems offline"
halting pipeline activity.

data.label: Activity During Shutdown
user_properties:
While the mainlines remained down CPC operated
some lateral lines.

During this they learned that there was not enough
written documentation of manual or low tech operating
procedures and were reliant on older employees
who had operated prior to heavy automation for
section operation.

data.label: Initial Access
user_properties:
Malicious cyber actors acquired employee user credentials 
for a VPN service externally.The employee had used the

credentials for an external service from where they are
suspected to have gotten.

The MCAs then gained access to the IT network through
the VPN service, which was thought to be out of service
and not properly monitored.



Once in the system the MCAs deployed DarkSide ransomware
and locked down the corporate IT system.

data.label: Pipeline Restart
user_properties:
CPS paid the ransom and eventually were able

to initiate restart on may11th, fully restarting

operations on may 12th.



Despite paying for the key CPC stated that it
did not fully undo what had been done and they
continued to work on their systems and reevaluate

some policies.


CPC cooperated with the authorities during this

incident aside from when they went out of contact
in advance of paying the ransom against FBI

recommendation.

meta.title: NotPetya Ransomware CAD Model
meta.description: A model of the 2017 worldwide attack by the Sanworm Team using the NotPetya Ransomware
meta.article: NotPetya is malware that was used by Sandworm Team in a worldwide attack starting on June 27, 2017. While NotPetya appears as a form of ransomware, its main purpose was to destroy data and disk structures on compromised systems; the attackers never intended to make the encrypted data recoverable.

data.label: Local Execution & Spread
user_properties:
Once the malware was downloaded onto a computer, it attempted to escalate its privileges and determine whether antivirus processes were running.
The malware then attempted to identify other computers on the same network. The malware would attempt to extract and execute a credential stealing 
program and/or escalate its privileges to achieve lateral movement to other computers on the network. If execution failed, the malware spread itself to 
other victim computers using either the exploit EtemalBlue or EternalRomance for SMBv1 to connect to other network nodes without credentials, then 
copy itself to those nodes and attempt to execute. After attempting lateral movement within the compromised computer's network, the malware searched
 for files ending with dozens of different file extensions and began encrypting those files on the compromised computer. Once the files were encrypted,
 the malware created a text file containing the ransom note inside every folder that contained encrypted files.

data.label: Initial Access
user_properties:
The NotPetya malware was disseminated initially using a popular Ukrainian accounting 
software called M.E.Doc. The software was periodically updated through an update 
server (the "Update Server"). The attackers rerouted internet traffic from the Update Server 
to their France-based server which delivered the malware to the victim computers. The 
attackers surreptitiously add malicious functionality to the files containing the software 
updates (the "Update Files") and computers receiving M.E.Doc software updates downloaded 
these Update Files, which at some point included the NotPetya malware.

data.label: Overview
user_properties:
On June 27, 2017 the malicious actors executed a
series of malware attacks to render the computer 
systems used by Ukrainian organizations inoperable, 
including banks, newspapers, and electricity companies. 
The "NotPetya" malware was used to target the electric 
sector. The NotPetya malware spread to connected 
networks belonging to other victim computer systems 
belonging to victims in other countries, including in 
the United States.

meta.title: 2023 Malicious Exploitation of Unitronics PLC's
meta.description: A model of the 2023 exploitation of PLCs used in Water and Wastewater Systems.
meta.article: In November & December of 2023, IRGC affiliated threat actors the CyberAv3ngers gained access to Unitronics PLC's in water and wastewater systems across the US. Unitronics Vision Series PLC's at the time came with a default password searchable via the user manual. The malicious actors gained access using these valid credentials to PLC's openly connected using the commonly used TCP port 20256 to the public internet.

data.label: Unitronics Vision Series PLC
user_properties: Israeli-made Unitronics Vision Series programmable logic controllers (PLCs)

data.label: Summary
user_properties:
In November & December of 2023, IRGC affiliated threat actors the CyberAv3ngers 
gained access to Unitronics PLC's in water and wastewater systems across the US.

The Unitronics Vision Series PLC's came with a built in HMI screen, once accessed
the malicious actors displayed threatening messages on the screens.


Unitronics Vision Series PLC's at the time came with the default password "1111"
which was also searchable through the user manual.

The malicious actors gained access using these valid credentials to PLC's openly
connected using the commonly used TCP port 20256 to the public internet.

meta.description: Model of one of the execution pathways of the BlackEnergy3 malware by the Sandworm Team during he 2015 Ukranian Electric Power Attack.
meta.article: The 2015 Ukraine Electric Power Attack was a Sandworm Team campaign during which they used BlackEnergy (specifically BlackEnergy3) and KillDisk to target and disrupt transmission and distribution substations within the Ukrainian power grid. This campaign was the first major public attack conducted against the Ukrainian power grid by Sandworm Team.

data.label: Standard Application Layer Protocol - ATTACK ICS
Overview
user_properties:
BlackEnergy is a malware toolkit that has been used by both criminal and APT actors. It dates back to at least 2007 
and was originally designed to create botnets for use in conducting Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, 
but its use has evolved to support various plug-ins. It is well known for being used during the confrontation between 
Georgia and Russia in 2008, as well as in targeting Ukrainian institutions. Variants include BlackEnergy 2 and 

BlackEnergy 3.

data.label: Loss of Productivity and Revenue - ATTACK ICS
Dissruption of Control
user_properties:
Threat actors use native remote access services and valid credentials to open breakers and 
disrupt power distribution to over 225,000 customers within three distribution areas for 6 hours.


After opening the breakers, threat actors deliver malicious firmware update to serial-to-Ethernet 
communications devices. The malicious updates render the converters inoperable, and sever 
connections between the control center and the substations.

meta.title: Purdue Model illustrated by D3FEND for OT artifacts
meta.description: This model presents an overview of the Purdue Model, using the D3FEND for OT ontology extensions.  A simplified view of the levels and typical components is on the left.  To the right is an expanded view of this, showing the D3FEND for OT relationships between the artifacts.

data.label: Purdue Model
user_properties:
The Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture (PERA), or "Purdue Model", is a reference architecture for enterprise control.  
It was developed by an industry consortium led by Purdue University and outlines several hierarchical levels of control starting
at the physical process (level 0) and rising up to the enterprise level (level 5).  Levels 0-3 represent the core operational 
technology domain (OT) parts of the architecture, whereas levels 4-5 are general purpose information technology (IT). The 
scope of time and space increase as the levels increase, with the nearest and most time-critical functions occurring at lower levels.

Since its initial definition and standardization in ISA-95, it has been interpreted and extended many times, but the basic 
hierarchical model is useful as an organizing principle. Here we include two frequently recommended DMZ layers.

In some cases, the original level names have been updated and the Purdue Model names are in brackets.

data.label: Purdue Level 5
user_properties: This level is for corporate wide strategic planning and analytics managing OT process. Planning time frame: months to years.

data.label: Purdue Level 3
user_properties: This level includes the outside edge of your control network. At this level, you may be aggregating several control networks together for higher level supervisory actions and trends. Operational time frame: hours to days.

data.label: Purdue Level 2
user_properties: This level includes the devices, interfaces, and supporting equipment that provide local view and control to the processes of a specific area. Operational time frame: seconds to minutes.

data.label: Purdue Level 1
user_properties: This level includes devices that are closest to the physical process while still providing the ability to make changes or decisions. Devices at this level are able to be programmed and communicate to other parts of the network. Operational time frame: milliseconds to seconds.

data.label: Purdue Level 0
user_properties: This level includes devices that are directly interacting with the physical environment and process. These include sensors, actuators, and other similar devices. Communication is through physical connection and devices are frequently mechanical in operation. Operational time frame: microseconds to seconds.

data.label: OT Create New Control Program Command
<Extension>
user_properties: This additional layer isolates the OT network from the IT network. Sometimes referred to as "Level 3.5" in "extended" versions of the Purdue Model. May contain intermediate systems and services shared between business and control networks.

data.label: <Extension>
user_properties: This additional layer isolates the IT network from the Internet. May contain proxy servers and public facing applications.

data.label: Purdue Level 4
user_properties: Business logistics systems for production scheduling and management at the plant-level. Incorporates production, material use, delivery, shipping, and inventory systems. Planning time frame: shifts to months.

data.label: Five key control program modifiication commands
user_properties:
D3FEND for OT models 40 additional types of OT-specific 
protocol messages in the OT Protocol Message taxonomy.

meta.description: High level overview of a model Y Tesla regenerative breaking system.

data.label: Rogue Wi-Fi Access Point
user_properties: An adversary could set up unauthorized Wi-Fi access points or compromise existing access points and, if the device connects to them, carry out network-based attacks such as eavesdropping on or modifying network communication.

data.label: Unintended Vehicle Network Message
user_properties: The adversary may try to send unintended messages on the in-vehicle network.

data.label: Initial Access
user_properties:
A Malicious Cyber Actor (MCA) exploits vulnerabilities in the software 
of EV Systems that are not updated. 


The MCA could also access the CAN BUS physically by connecting to 
the OBD-II port or accessing the wiring harness.


After they get access to the system, they impair the defenses of the EV 
to avoid being noticed by the car user 


The MCA then send messages to the ECU from the CAN BUS allowing 
the attacker to turn on or off critical systems in the EV.

data.label: Control over various Systems in EV
Exploit Aftermarket, Customer, or Dealer Equipment via OBD-II port
user_properties: Adversaries may take use aftermarket, customer, or dealer equipment as an initial OBD-II accessories, such as insurance dongles and fleet management dongles, may introduce a wireless ingress points to the vehicle through its OBD-II port.

data.label: Physical Modification via Wiring Harness
user_properties: The adversary can make physical modifications to the vehicle’s ECUs, wiring harnesses, and can replace ECUs.

data.label: Exploit via Removable Media
user_properties: Adversaries may gain initial access to an automotive environment by copying malware to removable media and taking advantage of Autorun features or automatic parsing of file (e.g., MP3s) when the device is inserted into a system and executes.

data.label: Malicious Cyber Actor
user_properties: Attacker has physical access to the EV

data.label: Physical Attacker chooses to attack via USB port, OBD-II port, or by accessing wiring harness
Manipulate Communications via V2X Spoofing
user_properties: If network traffic between the vehicle and a remote server or mobile device is not securely protected, then an attacker positioned on the network may be able to manipulate network communication without being detected.

data.label: Exploit via Radio Interface
user_properties: The vehicle may be targeted for exploitation through its interface to cellular networks or other radio interfaces.

data.label: Attack on Telematic Control Unit
user_properties:
A MCA establishes connection to EV through cellular network. 


The MCA then exploits zero-day vulnerabilities in the TCU by sending 
crafted telematic messages. 

The MCA then obtains root privileges to the TCU. 


After the TCU has been compromised the Attacker can now take control 
of the EV remotely and send messages to the ECU from the CAN Bus 
affecting the control of Electric Control Unit in the EV.

data.label: Exploitation via Remote Services
user_properties: Adversaries may attempt to log into a service specifically designed to accept remote connections. The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

data.label: Browser Compromise
user_properties: A browser compromise is when an adversary gains access to a system through a user visiting a website over the normal course of browsing. With this technique, the user's web browser is targeted for exploitation.

data.label: ECU Credential Dumping
user_properties: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password, from the operating system and software.

user_properties: Affects eCharge cloud infrastructure and allows remote unauthenticated users to execute arbitrary commands.

data.label: CVE-2024-37310
user_properties: Vulnerability in the EVerest open-source EV charging firmware stack could allow attackers to gain access to the CAN bus and compromise critical vehicle components.

data.label: CVE-2018-9311 and CVE-2018-9318
user_properties: TCUs in BMW vehicles allowed for potential remote attack via cellular network.

data.label: CVE-2023-34733
user_properties: A lack of exception handling in the Volkswagen Discover Media Infotainment System Software Version 0876 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via supplying crafted media files when connecting a device to the vehicle's USB plug and play feature.

data.label: CVE-2022-0878
user_properties: A vulnerability in the Combined Charging System (CCS), a communication protocol used by EVs and EVSE, can allow for unauthorized control of the charging process and compromise the integrity of the charging session.

data.label: CVE-2024-25994 and CVE-2024-25995
user_properties: An unauthenticated remote attacker can modify configurations to perform a remote code execution, gain root rights or perform an DoS due to improper input validation.

user_properties: By sending a specific reset UDS request via OBDII port of Skoda vehicles, it is possible to cause vehicle engine shutdown and denial of service of other vehicle components even when the vehicle is moving at a high speed. No safety critical functions affected.

meta.description: A model of the 2021 ransomware attack on the Colonial Pipeline Company (CPC)
meta.article: Malicious cyber actors acquired gained access to Colonial Pipeline's IT network and once in the system the MCAs deployed DarkSide ransomware and locked down the corporate IT system. On may 7th 2021 the Colonial Pipeline Company (CPC) learned they were victims of a ransomware cyber attack. In response CPC proactively took certain systems offline halting pipeline activity.

data.label: Pipeline Shutdown
user_properties:
On may 7th 2021 the Colonial Pipeline Company (CPC) 
learned they were victims of a ransomware cyber attack.


In response CPC "proactively took certain systems offline"
halting pipeline activity.

data.label: Activity During Shutdown
user_properties:
While the mainlines remained down CPC operated
some lateral lines.


During this they learned that there was not enough
written documentation of manual or low tech operating
procedures and were reliant on older employees
who had operated prior to heavy automation for
section operation.

data.label: Initial Access
user_properties:
Malicious cyber actors acquired employee user credentials 
for a VPN service externally.The employee had used the

credentials for an external service from where they are

suspected to have gotten.


The MCAs then gained access to the IT network through

the VPN service, which was thought to be out of service
and not properly monitored.



Once in the system the MCAs deployed DarkSide ransomware
and locked down the corporate IT system.

data.label: Pipeline Restart
user_properties:
CPS paid the ransom and eventually were able

to initiate restart on may11th, fully restarting

operations on may 12th.



Despite paying for the key CPC stated that it
did not fully undo what had been done and they
continued to work on their systems and reevaluate

some policies.


CPC cooperated with the authorities during this

incident aside from when they went out of contact
in advance of paying the ransom against FBI

recommendation.

meta.title: Triton Safety Instrumented System Attack
meta.description: A model of the 2017 Triton Safety Instrumented System Attack which targeted specific Triconex Safety Controllers.
meta.article: Triton Safety Instrumented System Attack was a campaign employed by TEMP.Veles which leveraged the Triton malware framework against a petrochemical organization. The malware and techniques used within this campaign targeted specific Triconex Safety Controllers within the environment.

data.label: External Remote Services (ICS)
user_properties: Adversaries may leverage external remote services as a point of initial access into your network. These services allow users to connect to internal network resources from external locations. Examples are VPNs, Citrix, and other access mechanisms. Remote service gateways often manage connections and credential authentication for these services.

data.label: Masquerading (ICS)
user_properties: Adversaries may use masquerading to disguise a malicious application or executable as another file, to avoid operator and engineer suspicion. Possible disguises of these masquerading files can include commonly found programs, expected vendor executables and configuration files, and other commonplace application and naming conventions. By impersonating expected and vendor-relevant files and applications, operators and engineers may not notice the presence of the underlying malicious content and possibly end up running those masquerading as legitimate functions.

data.label: Scripting (ICS)
user_properties: Adversaries may use scripting languages to execute arbitrary code in the form of a pre-written script or in the form of user-supplied code to an interpreter. Scripting languages are programming languages that differ from compiled languages, in that scripting languages use an interpreter, instead of a compiler. These interpreters read and compile part of the source code just before it is executed, as opposed to compilers, which compile each and every line of code to an executable file. Scripting allows software developers to run their code on any system where the interpreter exists. This way, they can distribute one package, instead of precompiling executables for many different systems. Scripting languages, such as Python, have their interpreters shipped as a default with many Linux distributions.
